extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and authors (including self-published authors) learning how to choose and use narrative point of view
extracted.subtask_short: choosing and using narrative point of view
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for selecting a narrative point of view (first, second, third, fourth, omniscient/limited) and applying it consistently in fiction and short-form writing. Covers genre conventions, common pitfalls (head-hopping, tonal drift), and formatting notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define who's telling the story (POV = who’s speaking / what they know / how they experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view is the angle your story is told from: who’s speaking, what they know, how they experience what’s happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose your POV early — it shapes what the reader sees and how connected they feel. The choice affects what information is available and controls the reader’s access to thoughts, knowledge, and emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay consistent with chosen point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you choose a point of view, you have to stay consistent with it. If you drift, even a little, readers feel it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid small slips (a thought the character couldn’t realistically have; a line that feels like it’s coming from outside the scene). If you need to change POV, do it cleanly (new scene, new chapter, or a clear break). Consistency should become invisible when handled well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not head-hop within a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: In limited perspectives (first person or third person limited), you cannot head hop within a scene — i.e., describe multiple people's inner thoughts in the same moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head-hopping breaks the illusion and confuses readers. Example anti-pattern provided: alternating internal access to Sarah and Tom in the same paragraph. Fix by keeping only the POV character’s internal thoughts and using observed behavior or dialogue for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person: choose omniscient vs limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Third person uses he/she/they/it. There are two main approaches: omniscient (narrator knows more than any single character and can access multiple minds or offer commentary) and limited (narration filters everything through a single character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omniscient allows god’s-eye view and commentary (more common in classics and picture books). Limited keeps close to one character and is widely used in modern fiction. Choose based on the reading experience you want to create.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person omniscient — when to use and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Third person omniscient narrator can dive into multiple characters’ thoughts, reveal secrets, and step back for commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Tolstoy's War and Peace and Melville's Moby-Dick. Less common in modern novels but useful for works that benefit from a broad or authoritative viewpoint; often appears in children’s picture books or narratives needing a ‘god’s-eye’ perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person limited — scope and prohibition on internal head-hopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person limited allows the narrator to see into only one character's mind at a time; you cannot head hop within a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous examples are The Great Gatsby and Harry Potter (experienced largely through one character). You may switch limited perspectives between scenes/chapters, but clearly delineate switches to avoid confusing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple third-person limited POVs — distinct narrators and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple 3rd person POVs require each narrator to only know what's in their heads; authors may switch narrator between scenes or chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure readers do not get confused about POV switches. Each POV must feel distinct in knowledge and voice. Practical recommendation: don't use more than 3–6 narrators in a story; first-time authors should use only 1–3 POVs. Poor transitions invite negative reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: First person POV — benefits and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: First person uses 'I' and filters everything through one person’s thoughts and perspective, offering strong immediacy and emotional closeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strength: pulls readers in fast, good for genres that rely on emotion (YA, romance). Risks: voice can become repetitive, overly introspective, or make the narrator unlikeable. Technical note: you don't need italicized thoughts — the narration itself is the character’s thought; still use quotation marks for dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second person POV — rarity and suitable contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Second person uses 'you' and addresses the reader/character directly. It's uncommon in literature but appears in notable works and formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works best in short stories, short-form creative writing, blogs, self-help, and text-based games. Famous example: Bright Lights, Big City. Use sparingly and typically for shorter pieces or experimental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth person POV / indefinite pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth person uses indefinite pronouns (one, someone, anybody, oneself) or sometimes a collective 'we' without 'I'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to express general behaviors or to avoid passive constructions. Less common in fiction; the main advantage is referring to general actions or depersonalized perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match POV to genre and desired reader experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres commonly favor different POVs because of the reader experience they create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: YA often uses first person for immediacy; fantasy/SF often uses third person for scope and worldbuilding; romance often uses third-person limited switching between lovers; mystery/thriller use third person to control information. These are patterns, not rules — break them intentionally if you have a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let POV determine what information to withhold
rubrics_metrics.description: Good POV is about what you include and what you intentionally hold back; limited perspectives benefit from omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In limited POVs, don't explain every motivation or reveal every thought. Stronger writing often allows readers to interpret events based on what the POV character can observe rather than narrating everything explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for unintentional shifts in tone / voice
rubrics_metrics.description: POV issues often manifest as subtle tone changes — a sentence sounding more formal, distant, or all-knowing than surrounding narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A helpful check is to read your work aloud. If a line feels like it’s coming from a different voice, it probably is and may indicate POV drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make POV transitions intentional and clearly marked
rubrics_metrics.description: If you shift perspectives, do it on purpose and make transitions clear to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scene breaks, chapter breaks, or other clear signals. Unclear transitions force readers to pause and figure out whose perspective they're in, breaking narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical formatting note for first person thoughts vs dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Since first-person narration is already inside the character’s head, you don't need to set thoughts apart (e.g., italics) as you might in third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Still use quotation marks for spoken dialogue. Avoid unnecessary formatting that separates the narrator’s internal voice from the narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and reading as a diagnostic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: If unsure which POV to choose, look at stories you already enjoy and analyze how they handle perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice what you’re allowed to see, what’s held back, and how close you feel to characters. Then apply those observations to your own writing and iterate until the POV fits the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: If breaking conventional patterns, do it deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking genre/POV expectations is acceptable only when the choice feels intentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers will accept unconventional POVs if they feel purposeful; they will push back if the break feels accidental or confusing. Ensure the technique serves the story.
